title: parse_iso_8601() performance
description:
Hi, thanks for the excellent package—this seems to be the most complete ISO 8601 parser in R.

I’m seeing a substantial performance gap compared to alternatives, even on valid ISO 8601 inputs. Notably, only `parsedate::parse_iso_8601()` parses the full set below (others fail on e.g. week/ordinal dates):
```
x <- c(
  "2026-04-02T02-04:40","2026-04-02T02:16-04:40",
  "2026-04-02T02:16:01-04:40","2026-04-02T02:16:01.5-04:40",
  "2026-04-02T02:16:01.123456-04:40","2026-04-02T06:16Z",
  "2026-04-02T06:16:01Z","20260402T0216-0440",
  "20260402T021601-0440","2026-04-02","2026-W14-4",
  "2026-092","2026-04-02T02:16","2026-04-02T02:16:01.123Z"
)

n <- 1e5
x1 <- x[sample.int(length(x), n, replace=TRUE)]
x2 <- sample.int(n, n) |> as.POSIXct() |> as.character()
microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  parse_iso_8601=parsedate::parse_iso_8601(x1),
  readr=readr::parse_datetime(x1),
  iso8601=iso8601::iso8601todatetime(x1),
  strptime=strptime(x2, '%F %T'),  ## fixed format, not ISO
  times=3L
) |> suppressWarnings() |> suppressMessages()

# Unit: milliseconds
#            expr      min        lq      mean    median        uq       max neval cld
#  parse_iso_8601 716.5955 719.05596 721.38917 721.51640 723.78599 726.05558     3 a  
#           readr  16.7511  16.77024  16.87561  16.78938  16.93786  17.08635     3  b 
#         iso8601 142.3865 147.68687 208.98686 152.98725 242.28704 331.58684     3   c
#        strptime 263.1330 264.07260 265.11696 265.01224 266.10897 267.20570     3   c
```

On my machine, `parse_iso_8601()` is ~4–40× slower.

[See full context on Stack Overflow.](https://stackoverflow.com/q/79925642/6574038)

Is this expected (due to broader ISO 8601 coverage), or are there optimization opportunities (e.g., fast paths for common formats)?

Cheers!

title: parsedate update from CRAN
description:
```
Dear maintainer,

Please see the problems shown on
<https://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_results_parsedate.html>.

The errors on the Debian check systems are from a recent system upgrade
to tzdata 2024b which did

   Names present only for compatibility with UNIX System V
   (last released in the 1990s) have been moved to 'backward'.

which includes CET, CST6CDT, EET, EST*, HST, MET, MST*, PST8PDT, and
WET.

Debian ships the names in 'backward' in a separate package tzdata-legacy
which is not installed "by default".

The comments in the tzdata 'backward' file say

# Although this file is optional and tzdb will work if you omit it by
# building with 'make BACKWARD=', in practice downstream users
# typically use this file for backward compatibility.

so clearly one cannot unconditionally assume that the backward
compatibility names will work.

Can you please change your code (typically tests) so that they do not
fail when the backward compatibility names are not available?

Please correct before 2024-12-09 to safely retain your package on CRAN.

Best wishes,
The CRAN Team
```

title: Feature suggestion: Add rounding of fractional hours or minutes
description:
Related to #43 

@gaborcsardi, I can imagine that not everyone would want fractional seconds unless they are coming in the seconds part of the time.

For example, if someone gives a fractional hour, I assume that they would want minutes and maybe seconds, but they probably don't want fractional seconds.  And similarly, if someone gives a fractional minutes, they probably want seconds, but they probably don't want fractional seconds.

My first thought is to add a `round_time` argument to `parse_iso_8601()`.  That argument would have six ways it could be provided:

* `TRUE` (my suggested default): Round fractions to one time unit more precise than what is given:
    * If fractional hours are given, round the minutes, seconds are 0.
    * If fractional minutes are given, round the seconds, fractional seconds are 0.
    * If fractional seconds are given, round to the nearest millisecond
* `FALSE`: No rounding, get full precision down to fractional seconds (even beyond milliseconds), if provided.
* One of "hours", "mins", "secs", "msec" which would round to those levels.

title: Fractional seconds are not captured
description:
``` r
library(parsedate)
# positive hour timezone with minutes and fractional seconds
dput(
  parse_iso_8601("2024-08-03T01:02:03.123+04:15")
)
#> structure(1722631623, class = c("POSIXct", "POSIXt"), tzone = "UTC")
# fractional seconds are not captured
dput(
  as.POSIXct("2024-08-03 01:02:03.123")
)
#> structure(1722661323.123, class = c("POSIXct", "POSIXt"), tzone = "")
```

title: Assigning wrong year to dates in the following format: month-dd-yy HH:MM
description:
For whatever reason, `parse_date()` assigns the year 2022 for dates in the following format: month-dd-yy HH:MM. Here are some examples of raw dates that get incorrectly parsed:
```
december-30-11 1:14 pm
january-04-10 11:02 am
november-14-08 7:27 am
```
Otherwise, very impressive parsing function!

title: No leading zero on hours leads to wrong year
description:
parsedate::parse_date("1900-01-01 01:10:21") gives "1900-01-01 01:10:21 UTC"
but
parsedate::parse_date("1900-01-01 1:10:21") gives "2021-01-01 01:10:21 UTC"

This appears to be the case with other formats of time.  If the hour element is a single digit it results in 1900 becoming 2021.

title: Parsing dates with explicit time zone codes
description:
Where the input has an explicit timezone, this is currently ignored.  Is there a possibility to recognize and apply explicit time zone codes in date strings?

``` r
library(parsedate)
#> Warning: package 'parsedate' was built under R version 4.0.5
ct <- Sys.time()
print(ct)
#> [1] "2021-07-08 14:40:32 NZST"
lt <- as.POSIXlt(ct)
print(lt)
#> [1] "2021-07-08 14:40:32 NZST"
print(lt[1,'zone'])
#> [1] "NZST"
ctc <- as.character(ct, usetz = TRUE)
print(ctc)
#> [1] "2021-07-08 14:40:32 NZST"
ltz <- Sys.timezone()
print(ltz)
#> [1] "Pacific/Auckland"
parse_date(ctc)
#> [1] "2021-07-08 14:40:32 UTC"
parse_date(ctc, default_tz = ltz)
#> [1] "2021-07-08 02:40:32 UTC"
.POSIXct(parse_date(ctc, default_tz = ltz), tz=ltz)
#> [1] "2021-07-08 14:40:32 NZST"
as.POSIXct(parse_date(ctc, default_tz = ltz), tz=ltz)
#> [1] "2021-07-08 02:40:32 UTC"
```

<sup>Created on 2021-07-08 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0)</sup>

The second to last form gets me the original date/time back again, but I have to have worked out that the relevant time zone is 'Pacific/Auckland' to get there.
My source data may have explicit time zone codes in the dates, but I don't have pre-knowledge of what values may be present.
So even if I had the information about mapping NZST to 'Pacific/Auckland' (or any other Abbreviation/Name combination), I would have to parse all the dates first to get this information out.  This rather defeats the purpose of using your wonderful little package to do it for me!

title: parse_date is succeptible to the 2038 bug
description:
I originally thought this was because Linus hated the future, but I see that It was because of an integer overflow.

``` r
# Last known day to work
parsedate::parse_date("01/19/2038 03:14:07 GMT")
#> [1] "2038-01-19 03:14:07 UTC"
# One second later will throw NA
parsedate::parse_date("01/19/2038 03:14:08 GMT")
#> [1] NA
# Two seconds later and we begin again 
parsedate::parse_date("01/19/2038 03:14:09 GMT")
#> [1] "1901-12-13 20:45:53 UTC"
```

title: Feature Request: add timezone argument
description: Is it possible to add a timezone argument or option so that returned objects can have a timezone other than the system timezone? So, if I parse dates in UTC they return as UTC not system tz. I see you have the helper function `with_tz` but this changes the absolute time. `lubridate::force_tz` has the functionality but as you mention elsewhere, it requires loading a lot of other packages.

title: parse_date on date before 1970
description:
Is parse_date supposed to handle dates before 1970 in MM-DD-YYYY or  MMM DD YYYY format?

Examples:
**After 1970 in MM-DD-YYYY works:**

> parse_date("04-15-1971")
> [1] "1971-04-15 UTC"
> **Before 1970 in YYYY-MM-DD works:**
> parse_date("1969-04-15")
> [1] "1969-04-15 UTC"
> **After 1970 in MMM DD YYYY works:**
> parse_date("apr 15 1970")
> [1] "1970-04-15 UTC"
> **Before 1970 in MM-DD-YYYY doesn't work:**
> parse_date("04-15-1969")
> [1] "2015-01-04 UTC"
> **Before 1970 in MMM DD YYYY doesn't work:**
> parse_date("april 15 1969")
> [1] "2016-04-15 UTC"

title: Date interpreted TZ incorrectly
description:
> parsedate::parse_date("2010-07-01")
[1] "2010-06-30 19:00:00 CDT"

CDT is UTC -5, so I think that's why it bumped my time 5 hours forward. But wouldn't it better to assume that the data is for the same timezone as the computer viewing it, unless otherwise specified?

As `parse_date` runs  `parse_iso_8601` it might be worth noting that the later by itself behaves as expected.

~~~
> parse_date("2017-10-12T11:32:45.026+00:00"); parse_date("2017-10-12T11:32:45+00:00")
[1] "2017-10-12 13:32:45 CEST"

title: parse_date(character(0)) gives error
description:
```R
parse_date(character(0))
#> Error during wrapup: parse_date argument must be character
```

The problem is due to `sapply`: if the input is `character(0)`, it returns `list()`:
https://github.com/gaborcsardi/parsedate/blob/a7f4b1e25a8d95778119c48fa39fd489424f2bd0/R/parsedate-package.r#L90

Just another reason to not use `sapply`. :)
